title: Quantifying Vegetation Dependence on Groundwater: Evidence From Northern China's Drylands
content:
Abstract

Groundwater is a critical source for vegetation in drylands, yet the quantification of vegetation dependence on groundwater (VDG) remains underexplored. Understanding this dependence is essential for unraveling vegetation-groundwater interactions and informing sustainable water resources management in drylands. This study constructed a vegetation response curve to depth to groundwater (DTG) by analyzing the relationship between DTG and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) at the pixel scale. A new method was developed to quantify VDG from the fitted NDVI–DTG response curve, where VDG was defined as the rate of NDVI change per unit change in normalized DTG at the inflection point of the NDVI–DTG response curve. VDG values were obtained for nine representative arid, semi-arid, and semi-humid regions in northern China (with an annual precipitation gradient of 200–800 mm). VDG shows pronounced spatial variation across the nine regions, with mean values decreasing from approximately 1.28 in the driest region to approximately 0.24 in the wettest region along the precipitation gradient. A strong negative correlation between annual precipitation (P) and VDG was identified (VDG = 2.08e−0.0037P), highlighting precipitation as a dominant regulator of VDG across regions. The research provides new empirical evidence for a deeper understanding of the effects of groundwater on vegetation, and also provides strong scientific support for groundwater management and ecological restoration with various annual precipitation amounts.
